tldr: This paper presents RoboGesture, a framework that captures meaning and rhythm directly from audio without text, enabling humanoid robots to generate real-time co-speech gestures while preventing self-collisions. By combining a robot-specific dataset of over 300 gesture categories with an MPC-based safety filter, it achieves safe, expressive interactive responses on physical hardware (Unitree G1).
hero_caption: Overall system architecture of RoboGesture: (a) pretraining the aligner to disentangle rhythm and semantics from audio tokens, (b) training a diffusion model to generate continuous motion from past motion and audio features, and (c) streaming deployment on a physical robot coupled with an upstream dialogue LLM and an MPC safety filter.
overview:
For natural human-humanoid interaction, robots must accompany speech with appropriate gestures (co-speech gestures) aligned with the rhythm and semantics of the audio. However, directly applying conventional avatar-oriented methods to physical robots runs into three critical barriers. First, semantically rich gesture datasets that account for robot joint limits and self-collisions are extremely scarce. Second, passing through text loses vocal nuances and pre-phonetic anticipation, while during online generation, models tend to rely on the momentum of past motion and ignore the audio cues (a phenomenon called "Modality Eclipse"). Third, physical hardware poses real-world risks of severe vibration and self-collision.

To tackle these challenges, the authors propose "RoboGesture," an integrated approach that co-designs data generation, model architecture, and low-level control. First, they retargeted over 300 gesture categories into the robot's joint space and automatically synthesized a 1,000-hour pseudo-dialogue dataset free of self-collisions via MPC. Next, they designed an aligner that hierarchically extracts rhythm and global semantics directly from raw audio tokens, and trained a continuous flow matching generator with "Anti-Inertia CFG Masking"—a technique that intentionally masks historical motion so the policy proactively responds to audio without relying on inertia. Finally, during inference, an MPC-based safety filter is applied, almost entirely preventing physical self-collisions.

Evaluations on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid (41 DOFs across the upper body and dexterous hands) showed state-of-the-art results in beat consistency and semantic appropriateness compared to baselines. Furthermore, the self-collision rate dropped dramatically from several percent in existing approaches down to the 0.1% range. With an ultra-fast generation speed of 120 FPS, the system achieved physical interaction seamlessly synchronized with spoken dialogue.
contributions: Construction of a 300+ gesture category library guaranteed for safety in robot joint space, along with an automated pipeline synthesizing a 1,000-hour large-scale semi-synthetic dataset
Proposal of a hierarchical aligner that extracts cadence, pre-phonetic anticipation, and global semantics directly from raw audio for low-latency, text-free motion generation
Design of a continuous flow matching motion generator equipped with Anti-Inertia CFG Masking to overcome excessive reliance on past motion (Modality Eclipse)
Realization of a full "listen, respond, and gesture" streaming dialogue system on a physical Unitree G1, reducing self-collision rates to 0.13% via a real-time MPC filter during inference

sections.heading: Why is humanoid gesturing difficult, and what does this work aim for?
sections.summary: Synchronized and semantically meaningful gestures are essential for natural human-robot interaction, but three major hurdles exist: data scarcity, model inertia that ignores audio cues, and hardware-specific collision risks. This work proposes an integrated framework co-designing data, modeling, and control to generate safe, real-time motion directly in the robot's joint space.
sections.details:
In settings such as eldercare, education, and collaborative work, it is vital for humanoid robots to listen to human speech and interact in real time with appropriate bodily gestures. However, bringing this capability to real physical robots rather than on-screen avatars faces three deep-rooted obstacles.

First is the scarcity of semantically rich audio-motion paired data. Existing datasets focus mostly on rhythmic beat gestures and contain very few gestures with concrete semantic meanings. Conventional methods have relied on intermediate text representations or heavy post-processing, which compromises temporal fidelity and immediate responsiveness.

Second is the problem of "Modality Eclipse" during online generation. When generating motions frame-by-frame in a streaming setup, the model often learns a shortcut: simply carrying over the momentum of the immediate past motion (kinematic inertia), thereby ignoring subtle incoming audio cues.

Third is the sim-to-real gap between avatars and physical hardware. The standard approach—generating motion in human skeletal space and retargeting it online to the robot via PD control—frequently causes jitter from abrupt joint accelerations and dangerous self-collisions where the hands strike the torso.

To overcome these hurdles, this paper builds a framework trained and optimized directly in "robot joint space" from the ground up. By combining collision-free large-scale data synthesis, a text-free hierarchical audio aligner, an inertia-breaking generation strategy, and an MPC safety filter at inference time, the framework delivers safe, highly responsive interaction on physical hardware.

sections.heading: Moving from CG avatar animation to real robot control
sections.summary: Social modeling for conversational robots has shifted from rule-based systems to deep learning, but avatar-oriented generation methods ignore physical constraints and safety. Furthermore, recent co-speech gesture methods rely heavily on text and post-processing, making them ill-suited for low-latency streaming.
sections.details:
Here, we review the evolution of social robotics and co-speech gesture generation.

### Social Interaction between Humans and Humanoids
While virtual avatar research has explored highly immersive dialogue, a substantial gap separates unconstrained avatar environments from physical robots. Previously, generating motions in human skeletal space and retargeting them onto robots later was common practice. However, this invariably leads to joint limit violations, kinematic singularities, and self-collisions. Rule-based or Behavior Tree approaches are safe and interpretable, but they cannot replicate the fluid flexibility of natural conversation or the subtle synchrony between voice and gesture. Therefore, this research abandons post-hoc retargeting and adopts direct multimodal learning within the robot's joint space representation from the outset.

### Co-speech Gesture Generation
From early rule-based and statistical models, deep learning became dominant with the introduction of datasets like BEAT. Recent works (such as LivelySpeaker, DiffSHEG, Semantic Gesticulator, and SemTalk) pursue semantic-motion alignment, but many rely on text or post-processing via CLIP global feature extraction or LLM-based motion retrieval. Going through text strips away intonation—such as whether "Really?" rises or falls—and makes it difficult to capture "pre-phonetic anticipation," where the body begins moving just before speech starts. Furthermore, retrieval-based methods incur high computational overhead, making them impractical for streaming interaction. This work directly tokenizes raw audio to disentangle semantics and rhythm, enabling completely text-free, low-latency streaming motion generation.

sections.heading: RoboGesture's core technologies: Hierarchical Aligner, Flow Matching, and MPC Filter
sections.summary: The system comprises three components: an aligner that hierarchically extracts rhythm and semantics from audio tokens, a flow matching generator designed to counteract past inertia, and an MPC filter that eliminates self-collisions during inference. It achieves end-to-end streaming control over 41 DOFs (upper body and hands) on the Unitree G1.
sections.details:
The target platform is the Unitree G1 humanoid equipped with BrainCo dexterous hands, offering 41 DOFs (17 for the upper body and 24 across both hands). The system generates gestures in a streaming fashion using 1-second chunks (30 frames).

### 3.1 Hierarchical Semantic-Acoustic Aligner
To extract temporally accurate motion cues directly from audio without text, audio is converted into hierarchical tokens using the Mimi codec. Using a Transformer-based aligner, shallow layers route features to an auxiliary rhythm prediction head that detects audio onsets, while deep layers feed features to a semantic head performing discrete classification over 300 gesture categories. This creates a clear division of labor: shallow layers handle millisecond-level beats, while deep layers capture global semantics such as communicative intent and emotion. The system can even capture pre-phonetic anticipation, such as leaning back slightly while inhaling before shouting.

### 3.2 Streaming Conditional Motion Generator
The motion generation module adopts a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) operating in continuous space with Conditional Flow Matching (CFM), avoiding the quantization loss and compounding errors seen in discrete autoregressive models. A dual condition injection mechanism is used to counteract Modality Eclipse:
- **Frame-level Micro-Alignment (Cross-Attention)**: Shallow (rhythm) and deep (local semantic) features from the aligner, along with the previous 2 seconds ($T_{hist}=60$ frames) of historical motion, are fed into cross-attention as Keys and Values to achieve smooth transitions and temporal synchrony.
- **Global Modulation (FiLM)**: Compact global semantic directives extracted by the aligner are injected into the intermediate layers of the DiT via Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM). This firmly establishes the emotional and attitudinal tone without getting drowned out by local joint noise.

### 3.3 MPC-based Safety Filter
Passing raw outputs from the generative model directly to hardware carries a risk of self-collision due to stochastic variance. During inference, a quadratic program (QP) with geometric self-collision constraints is solved frame by frame in real time (taking about 5.6 ms per frame with the OSQP solver), balancing joint velocity, target trajectory tracking, and motion smoothness. This reduces the proportion of self-colliding frames from 4.16% down to 0.13%.

### 3.4 Training Strategy and Objectives
Training is conducted in two stages. In Stage 1, the DiT is frozen, and 1,000 hours of data are used to optimize only the aligner's rhythm regression loss and semantic classification loss (cross-entropy). In Stage 2, the DiT is unfrozen, and the entire network is trained using a velocity matching loss combined with a kinematic consistency loss ($\mathcal{L}_{kin}$) to preserve smoothness. During this stage, "Anti-Inertia CFG Masking" is applied by randomly dropping the historical motion condition with a 15% probability. Forcing cold starts without motion history compels the model to actively mine generative cues from the audio modality. Additionally, the 24 DOFs of the hands are weighted with $w_{hand}=4.0$ to ensure delicate finger movements are preserved.

sections.heading: 300 robot-tailored classes: An automated pipeline for large-scale semi-synthetic data
sections.summary: To overcome the self-collisions and robot incompatibilities in existing datasets, the authors built "RoboGesture," a high-quality library of over 300 gesture categories. They also developed a pipeline leveraging LLMs and TTS to synthesize 1,000 hours of collision-free, robot-kinematically-optimized audio-motion pairs.
sections.details:
The performance of generative models hinges on the scale and quality of training data. However, existing gesture datasets (such as SeG) are grounded in human skeletal anatomy. Replaying them on a robot leads to arms penetrating the torso or motions failing due to limited neck range of motion.

### 4.1 Retargeting and Collision Avoidance
To map human motion capture data accurately to the Unitree G1 and BrainCo hands, an improved GMR was used for the body, and Dex-Retargeting was employed for the hands. Non-uniform scaling based on finger length ratios and redefining relative vectors from wrist to fingertips allowed the robot hands to perform intended gestures reliably. The data was then filtered through the MPC module to retain only clean, collision-free demonstrations.

### 4.2 RoboGesture Dataset
Building on templates from SeG and EgoGesture, the authors established over 300 gesture classes informed by daily conversation surveys. Missing actions or clips difficult to reproduce on hardware were re-recorded using an in-house full-body motion capture system. Every sample was verified via playback on the physical robot to validate tracking fidelity and physical feasibility.

### 4.3 Semi-Synthetic Data Generation Pipeline
Using this base library, large-scale data was automatically synthesized in five steps:
- **Scenario Generation**: An LLM generated diverse, emotionally expressive conversational scenarios and dialogue lines.
- **Gesture Tagging**: Gestures matching the semantic meaning of the dialogue were selected from RoboGesture, with optimal insertion timings assigned.
- **Multimodal Synthesis**: Emotion-conditioned TTS generated speech with word-level timestamps, while a model trained on BEAT synthesized rhythmic beat gestures.
- **Temporal Blending**: Mimicking human behavior, semantic gestures were scheduled to start 0.4 seconds ahead of spoken keywords, smoothly blended with beat motions using quintic splines.
- **Safety Optimization**: Collision-avoidance optimization was applied to all blended trajectories, yielding a fully collision-free 1,000-hour training corpus.

sections.heading: Rigorous benchmark and physical experiments: Superior rhythm and semantic expression
sections.summary: On BEAT and the newly introduced SemanticBEAT benchmark, RoboGesture outperformed state-of-the-art baselines across objective metrics including FGD, beat consistency, and collision rate. It also earned the highest preference in user studies, demonstrating low-latency, safe co-speech gesturing during streaming interaction on a physical Unitree G1.
sections.details:
Evaluation was conducted both on standard simulation benchmarks and through real-world interaction tasks on the Unitree G1. The method was compared against four modern baselines: LivelySpeaker, DiffSHEG, SemTalk, and Semantic Gesticulator (SG).

### Quantitative Results
On the BEAT dataset, RoboGesture achieved top scores in Fréchet Gesture Distance (FGD), measuring motion naturalness, as well as the best results in Beat Consistency (BC) and joint position error (MSE). Notably, while baseline methods produced self-collision rates of several percent (or even higher), RoboGesture achieved an exceptionally low rate of 0.13% to 0.88%. While some baselines like SG showed high diversity scores (DIV), qualitative inspection revealed that this was an artifact of jittery and physically collapsed motions.

### User Study
In a user study evaluating 200 comparison pairs across four criteria—Rhythm Alignment (RA), Semantic Appropriateness (SA), Physical Consistency & Hand Expressiveness (PHC), and Overall Preference (OP)—the proposed method won clear majorities over all baselines. Participants favored the suppression of high-frequency jitter and the natural timing of semantically coherent hand gestures (such as an "OK" sign).

### Ablation Findings
Ablation experiments highlighted several critical components:
- **Data Scale**: Completely removing the semi-synthetic data led to a dramatic collapse in semantic gestures and finger detail, reducing outputs to basic rhythm-matching motions.
- **Past Motion and FiLM**: Removing past motion context produced discontinuous motion jumps, while removing FiLM global modulation degraded overall emotional expression.
- **CFG and Aligner Classification**: Removing Anti-Inertia CFG caused the model to lazily repeat past motion history, and eliminating semantic classification in the aligner significantly impaired semantic extraction from audio.
- **Kinematic Loss and Safety Filter**: The kinematic loss ($\mathcal{L}_{kin}$) was directly tied to hand smoothness, while the inference-time filter was essential for eliminating residual minor collisions and unnatural poses.

### Physical Robot System Evaluation
The complete dialogue pipeline—ASR, LoRA-fine-tuned Qwen3-4B-Instruct, TTS, and the motion generator—was deployed on the Unitree G1. The motion generator processed a 1-second chunk in about 0.25 seconds (equivalent to 120 FPS), and the MPC filter solved in just 5.6 ms per frame. The overall interaction latency was dominated by the linguistic upstream (such as ASR endpointing taking ~0.5 seconds and initial TTS chunk generation). The motion stack itself easily cleared the robot's 30 Hz control loop to track speech in real time.

sections.heading: Summary and future outlook
sections.summary: By co-designing data, modeling, and low-level control, RoboGesture establishes a framework for humanoids to interact safely in real time with meaningful gestures. Real-world experiments demonstrated high interactive quality across both rhythm and semantics.
sections.details:
This paper presented RoboGesture, an end-to-end framework enabling humanoid robots to engage in truly natural interaction with humans.

The core achievements can be summarized in three points:
1. A unified system co-designed from data collection and model architecture to physical control strictly from a robot-centric perspective
2. A robust pipeline producing over 300 safe gesture categories and 1,000 hours of semi-synthetic training data
3. A continuous-space motion policy that overcomes historical inertia to directly translate audio semantics and rhythm into smooth robot trajectories

Experiments on the physical Unitree G1 confirmed that the system outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in safety, rhythmic synchronization, and semantic accuracy. This research provides a key stepping stone toward evolving humanoid robots from simple machinery into attentive social companions.

sections.heading: Appendix: Hardware deployment details, empirical proof of Modality Eclipse, and metrics
sections.summary: The appendix details the fundamental differences between avatars and physical robots, provides the dialogue system implementation and latency breakdown, details perturbation experiments validating Modality Eclipse, and offers formal metric definitions.
sections.details:
The appendix presents essential supplementary experiments and implementation details that substantiate the paper's claims.

### Necessity of Learning Directly in Robot Space
Conventional approaches that generate motions in human skeletal space before retargeting them to robots trigger a "cascade of risks": joint limit violations and torque saturation due to kinematic mismatches, computational latency from online retargeting, and self-collisions because volumes are ignored. Learning directly within the robot's joint space is an essential design choice for achieving both hardware safety and low latency.

### Physical System Setup and Latency Breakdown
In the language module, Qwen3-4B-Instruct is fine-tuned using LoRA to prepend emotion tags like "[excited]" or "[warm]" to its response text. This prompts the TTS engine to generate more expressive, colloquial speech and provides clear social context to the downstream gesture generator. The latency bottleneck lies in the language pipeline (such as the 0.5-second ASR silence detection threshold and TTS first-chunk generation), while the motion generation module itself runs in ~0.25 seconds per 1-second chunk, providing ample real-time headroom.

### Quantitative Proof of Modality Eclipse
To evaluate the tendency of models to ignore audio and follow recent kinematic momentum, perturbation experiments were conducted by swapping audio while keeping past motion fixed, and vice versa. In a baseline lacking the semantic-acoustic aligner, output variations caused by swapping past motion were 4.57 times larger than those caused by swapping audio, showing extreme reliance on past inertia. In contrast, the full proposed model reduced this ratio to 2.04, demonstrating balanced audio conditioning. Furthermore, when audio was randomly shuffled, the proposed model's FGD degraded sharply from 0.624 to 9.151 (proving it actively listens to the audio), whereas the inertia-dominated baseline showed almost no metric change (proving it was ignoring the audio all along).

takeaways: Disentangling rhythm (shallow layers) and global semantics (deep layers) directly from audio tokens without text enables low-latency gesture generation that captures intonation and pre-phonetic anticipation.

In streaming gesture generation, models readily fall into "Modality Eclipse" by leaning on past motion inertia; randomly dropping past context (Anti-Inertia Masking) serves as an effective countermeasure.
Rather than retargeting avatar animation after the fact, curating datasets and training directly within the robot's joint space is key to preventing self-collisions and succeeding on real hardware.

To maintain near-100% physical safety while tolerating stochastic variations from generative models, inserting a lightweight quadratic program (MPC safety filter) during inference is an effective hybrid architecture.
limitations: The control scope is limited to the upper body and hands (41 DOFs), excluding whole-body weight shifting, walking, navigation, and object manipulation.
Heavy reliance on automated semi-synthetic data means expressiveness may be constrained by biases in the upstream LLM/TTS models and the pre-defined 300 gesture categories.

While the motion generation stack runs at 120 FPS, the perceived latency of the overall interaction system is still dominated by linguistic components (around 1.5 seconds for ASR silence detection and LLM/TTS first-chunk generation).
